title: Belgian PM's Chocolate India Gate Melts En Route as India and Belgium Reset Ties After 20 Years
excerpt: Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever's gift of a chocolate India Gate sculpture for PM Modi did not survive the journey, but the two leaders used his first visit in two decades to sign defense and trade agreements.
body:
• Belgian PM Bart De Wever's India visit marks the first by a Belgian head of government in 20 years, signaling a diplomatic reset.
  • A chocolate replica of India Gate, honoring Indian soldiers who fought in Flanders Fields during World War I, melted during transit to New Delhi.
  • India and Belgium signed several agreements covering defense cooperation, renewable energy, cybercrime and diplomatic training.
  • Bharat Forge's defense unit and France's Thales signed a deal to manufacture 70-mm rocket systems in India, with the first unit expected by early 2027.

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever arrived in New Delhi this week for the first visit by a Belgian head of government in 20 years — and brought along a diplomatic gift that never made it to the table.

Speaking at a joint press conference with Prime Minister Narendra Modi at Hyderabad House on September 3, De Wever revealed that a sculpture of India Gate, crafted entirely from Belgian chocolates, had melted during transit. "Chocolate is excellent for diplomacy, but not excellent for diplomatic travel, we noticed," he said with a smile, adding that a backup version remains in Belgium and will eventually be delivered.

A Tribute to Shared Wartime History

The choice of India Gate was deliberate. De Wever said the chocolate replica featured an enlarged inscription commemorating the more than 9,000 Indian soldiers who fought and died in Flanders Fields during the First World War. "More than a century ago, Indian soldiers travelled thousands of miles to fight on Belgian soil, and we have not forgotten this. We have not forgotten their courage and their sacrifice," he said.

The gesture underscored a theme running throughout the visit: that India and Belgium share deep, if sometimes overlooked, historical connections.

Defense Deals and Strategic Agreements

Beyond the chocolate anecdote, the visit produced tangible outcomes. India and Belgium exchanged several memoranda of understanding covering defense cooperation, renewable energy, cybercrime and diplomatic training.

The bilateral talks covered the full spectrum of India-Belgium relations, including trade, technology, semiconductors, critical minerals and security cooperation. Both leaders reaffirmed their shared commitment to combating terrorism.

A significant defense deal was also finalized on the sidelines. Bharat Forge's defense subsidiary, Kalyani Strategic Systems, signed an agreement with Thales — the French defense firm that manufactures 70-mm rocket systems through its Belgian unit — to establish production capability for the same systems in India. The Indian Army already uses these rockets, and the first fully assembled unit produced domestically is expected by early 2027.

Belgium Makes Its Case

De Wever acknowledged the 20-year gap in high-level visits was "too long" and praised India's transformation, describing it as "the world's largest democracy," the "fastest-growing major economy" and a rising "geopolitical factor."

He positioned Belgium as a natural economic partner despite the difference in scale, highlighting his country's status as one of the world's most open and internationally connected economies. Belgian Defence Minister Theo Francken also accompanied the delegation.

After concluding official meetings in New Delhi, De Wever traveled to Mumbai to engage with stakeholders in the diamond, ports and logistics industries — sectors where India-Belgium trade flows are particularly strong. Belgium is already one of the world's largest diamond trading hubs, and India is the global leader in diamond cutting and polishing.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The visit comes in the context of ongoing India-EU free trade agreement negotiations, which could significantly affect the Indian diaspora across Europe. De Wever delivered a keynote address at a Confederation of Indian Industry business event framed around the India-EU FTA. Stronger bilateral ties could translate into expanded business, research and educational opportunities for Indians in Belgium and across the EU.

As for the chocolate India Gate, De Wever left India with a new diplomatic ambition: "One way or another, I will get it to Prime Minister Modi in one piece."
nri_angle: The India-Belgium diplomatic reset and India-EU FTA talks could expand business and educational opportunities for the Indian diaspora in Europe.
author: Diaspora Desk
